project.name: mruby
project.commit_note: Stage 01 reproduced against the staged checkout under `gt_results/secbench_oss_mruby.ossfuzz-42532420/_work/src`, whose `HEAD` is the metadata vulnerable commit `219cfd63e151360efe664728e3b5dbcf6e102d44`, so all locations below use this exact vulnerable line map.

classification.classification_note: The saved crash is an 8-byte out-of-bounds read in the SWAR substring-search helper `mrb_memsearch_ss()`. The helper scans the haystack in 64-bit chunks while only bounding the loop by logical string length, not by the remaining readable width of the 8-byte loads.

bug_description.original: A heap-buffer-overflow in src/string.c's mrb_memsearch_ss: the function performs an 8-byte out-of-bounds read past a heap-allocated string buffer while performing substring search/split (seen via mrb_memsearch / mrb_str_split_m). This can lead to crashes or information disclosure/other undefined behavior during string search/split operations.
bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json issue_description / default_crash_trace.txt / sanitizer_trace.txt / reproduction_report.json / patch.diff / staged vulnerable source snapshot
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 8` at `src/string.c:609` in `mrb_memsearch_ss()` while the staged vulnerable `mruby` CLI executed the saved 40-byte Ruby program `"                            ".split"  "`. `mrb_load_detect_file_cxt()` reads the file as Ruby source, not a RITE binary, and execution reaches `String#split` with an explicit two-space separator, so `mrb_str_split_m()` takes the string-delimiter branch. In that branch the vulnerable source materializes `str_len = RSTRING_LEN(str)` and `pat_len = RSTRING_LEN(spat)` as 28 and 2 for the exact witness, initializes `idx = 0`, and then calls `mrb_memsearch(..., RSTRING_PTR(str)+idx, str_len - idx)`, so the first search window length passed as haystack `n` is source-grounded at 28 bytes. `mrb_memsearch()` only checks whether the needle length exceeds the current window length and then dispatches to `mrb_memsearch_ss()`. In the vulnerable helper, `ys` and `ys + m - 1` are cast to `bitint*`, and the loop condition is only `i < n`; with `n = 28` and 8-byte strides, the loop still reaches `i = 24`, where line 609 performs a full word load from the final partial chunk. The expression `(*s0 ^ first) | (*s1 ^ last)` therefore extends past the readable haystack bytes into the heap redzone. The fix confirms this missing bound by replacing the raw word loads with bounded `memcpy()` reads under `lim = n - MAX(m, sizeof(bitint))` and a bytewise tail fallback.

source.description: First project-side read of the attacker-controlled PoC file into mruby's source-loader buffer.
source.value_from: The saved `poc` is the exact 40-byte Ruby source string `"                            ".split"  "`. Because the file is shorter than `DETECT_SIZE`, this read materializes the whole witness into `leading.b` and sets `bufsize = 40`.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer crash site. The SWAR compare reads 8-byte words from the current haystack and the one-byte-shifted tail pointer without checking that 8 bytes remain readable.
sink.note: The symbolized `default_crash_trace.txt` reports `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow` at `src/string.c:609:24` in `mrb_memsearch_ss`, with `READ of size 8` on address `0x503000000388` at the end of a 30-byte heap region `[0x503000000370, 0x50300000038e)`. The separate saved `sanitizer_trace.txt` shows the same line reached on a different short region (29 bytes). Both artifacts support the same sink: a final 8-byte word read issued from an end-of-buffer position permitted by the loop.

root_cause.code: for (mrb_int i=0; i < n; i+=sizeof(bitint), s0++, s1++) {
root_cause.description: Root cause. The SWAR loop is bounded only by logical haystack length `n`, not by the remaining readable width required for the 8-byte loads from `s0` and `s1`.
root_cause.note: The bundled fix adds `lim = n - MAX(m, sizeof(bitint))`, iterates only while `i < lim`, and handles the tail bytewise. That patch directly confirms the missing bound on the vulnerable loop.

tainted_value_origin.description: The executed Ruby call `.split"  "` is unpacked into C locals, materializing the attacker-chosen separator string and split limit state used by the vulnerable search path.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: For the exact PoC `"                            ".split"  "`, this call receives one optional argument, so `argc = 1`, `spat` is the two-space string `"  "`, and no explicit limit is supplied.

parser_admitted.description: Sample-specific admission gate. The witness is plain Ruby source, not a RITE bytecode file, so this predicate routes it into the text parser/executor path.

admitted_location.code: return mrb_load_exec(mrb, mrb_parse_file_continue(mrb, fp, leading.b, bufsize, c), c);

evidence_limitations: Stage 02 remained source-grounded and did not rerun or instrument the fixed build. `patch_resolves` below is based on the staged diff's direct repair of the missing loop bound, not on dynamic fixed-version validation.

The saved crash artifacts do not settle one unique haystack size or address for the crashing search window: `default_crash_trace.txt` records a 30-byte region with full symbols, while `sanitizer_trace.txt` records a separate 29-byte region without symbolized frames. The staged source is sufficient to ground the invariant suffix used here: once the search window is shorter than 32 bytes, the vulnerable `i < n` loop still reaches `i = 24` and line 609 issues an out-of-bounds 8-byte read.

fine_trace.note: Source. The staged CLI reproduction opens the saved `poc` file and reads its full 40-byte Ruby program `"                            ".split"  "` into `leading.b`. This is the first project statement that materializes attacker-controlled bytes on the crashing path.

The witness is admitted as Ruby source, not a RITE binary: it is shorter than a full binary header, does not begin with `RITE`, and contains no NUL byte. Control therefore flows into `mrb_parse_file_continue(...leading.b, bufsize...)`, which is the only continuation that can execute the scripted `.split` call.

depends_on.via: bufsize < sizeof(leading.h) || memcmp(leading.h.binary_ident, RITE_BINARY_IDENT, sizeof(leading.h.binary_ident)) != 0 || memchr(leading.b, '\0', bufsize) == NULL

fine_trace.note: The executed Ruby method call is unpacked into C locals. For the exact witness, `mrb_str_split_m()` receives the left string as `str`, materializes one optional argument `spat = "  "`, and leaves `lim` unspecified, which sets up string-delimiter splitting instead of the default whitespace mode.

None of the whitespace-splitting conditions fire: the PoC provides a String separator, and its length is 2 rather than the single-space special case. `split_type` therefore stays `string`, which is the branch that later calls `mrb_memsearch()`.

At entry to the string-delimiter branch, the vulnerable code materializes the receiver length and separator length that define the first search window. For the exact witness, `str_len` is 28 spaces, `pat_len` is the two-byte separator, and `idx` starts at 0.

fine_trace.code: end = mrb_memsearch(RSTRING_PTR(spat), pat_len, RSTRING_PTR(str)+idx, str_len - idx);
fine_trace.note: The first string-search call forwards the separator bytes and the current receiver window into `mrb_memsearch()`. Because `idx` is still 0 here, the call passes `str_len - idx = 28` as the haystack length `n` used by the downstream search helper.

The wrapper only rejects degenerate cases such as `m > n`, equal-length full compare, empty needle, or single-byte search. With the witness values `m = 2` and `n = 28`, control falls through into `mrb_memsearch_ss()` without any check that the remaining haystack can safely satisfy the helper's 8-byte word loads.

The SWAR helper aliases the current haystack start as `s0` and a one-byte-shifted tail pointer as `s1`. Because the PoC separator length is `m = 2`, `s1` starts at `ys + 1`, so each loop iteration will attempt to read 8 bytes from two overlapping positions near the end of the same heap string.

fine_trace.code: for (mrb_int i=0; i < n; i+=sizeof(bitint), s0++, s1++) {
fine_trace.note: Root cause. The loop bound uses only logical haystack length `n`, so it keeps advancing in 8-byte steps while any byte remains. From step 6 the executed call passes `n = 28`, so the loop runs at `i = 0`, `8`, `16`, and `24`; the final entry still executes even though fewer than 8 readable bytes remain for `*s0` and even fewer for the one-byte-shifted `*s1`.

Sink. On the final iteration from step 9, this expression dereferences `s0` and `s1` as full 8-byte words near the end of the short heap search window. The symbolized saved crash trace reports the resulting `READ of size 8` at `src/string.c:609:24` on `0x503000000388`, and that 30-byte region ends at `0x50300000038e`, so the 8-byte load extends past the allocation and overlaps the right redzone. The separate raw sanitizer trace preserves the same line and access class on a 29-byte region.

allocation_context.note: The symbolized `default_crash_trace.txt` attributes one crashing short region to `mrb_str_times()` via `str_new()` / `str_init_normal_capa()`. The separate saved `sanitizer_trace.txt` preserves the same crash class at line 609 but not symbolized allocation frames, so Stage 02 does not claim more specific upstream runtime shaping than the symbolized stack supports.

format.name: Ruby source file
format.contract: The verified trigger semantics are limited to the exact saved witness `"                            ".split"  "`: a 28-space receiver string literal followed by `.split` with a two-space String literal argument. The file must remain valid Ruby source that keeps the explicit separator length at 2 so `mrb_str_split_m()` stays on the string-delimiter path instead of the omitted/nil or single-space whitespace path.
